questions.q: What does .str.strip() remove from a text column?
options: Leading and trailing whitespace only — not spaces in the middle of a value
All spaces anywhere in the string, including in the middle
All numbers from the string
The entire string's content
questions.explain: strip() removes only the invisible padding at the start and end of a value — the exact kind of stray space that breaks exact-match filters and comparisons.

questions.q: Why does ' West' (with a leading space) fail to match a filter looking for 'West'?
options: Pandas treats them as two completely different strings, even though they look identical to a human reader
Pandas automatically ignores leading spaces when filtering
This never actually happens in practice
Only trailing spaces cause this issue, never leading spaces
questions.explain: String comparison is exact — a leading space makes ' West' a genuinely different string from 'West', which is exactly why .str.strip() matters before filtering or joining.

questions.q: What does .str.title() do to a string?
options: Capitalizes the first letter of each word
Converts the entire string to uppercase
Converts the entire string to lowercase
Removes all whitespace from the string
questions.explain: title() capitalizes the first letter of each word — 'jordan lee' becomes 'Jordan Lee'.

questions.q: Why does the order matter in df["col"].str.strip().str.title()?
options: Stripping first ensures .title() capitalizes the actual first letter, rather than incorrectly treating a leading space as the start of the word
The order never actually matters for these two methods
.title() must always run before .strip()
Chaining string methods together is not allowed in Pandas
questions.explain: Running .title() on '  alex rivera' before stripping would capitalize incorrectly around the leading space — stripping first avoids that issue.

questions.q: How do you rename a column using .rename()?
options: Pass a dictionary with the old column name as the key and the new name as the value, e.g. df.rename(columns={"old": "New"})
Assign directly to df.columns[0] with a string
Renaming columns is not possible in Pandas
Use .str.rename() on the column itself
questions.explain: rename() takes a columns argument as a dictionary mapping old names to new ones — the same key-value dictionary shape introduced in Lesson 5.
